notes.front: What is a rehost migration (lift and shift)?
notes.back: Moving workloads from a source to a target environment with minor or no modifications or refactoring.
notes.explanation: The only changes made are the minimum the workloads need in order to operate in the target environment.
notes.example: Like moving house with every piece of furniture unchanged: a file server runs on a Compute Engine instance just as it ran in the data centre.
notes.evidence: In a rehost migration, you move workloads from a source environment to a target environment with minor or no modifications or refactoring. The modifications you apply to the workloads to migrate are only the minimum changes you need to make in order for the workloads to operate in the target environment.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, Migrate to Google Cloud: Get started, “Rehost: lift and shift”

notes.front: What is a replatform migration (lift and optimise)?
notes.back: Lifting existing workloads into the cloud and then optimising them for the new cloud environment.
notes.explanation: The guide says it suits organisations that want to use all the core competencies of the cloud.
notes.example: Like rehosting, with a second step: once the app has moved, it is adjusted so it can grow and shrink with demand.
notes.evidence: In a replatform migration, you lift the existing workloads and then optimize them for the new cloud environment. A replatform migration is best for organizations that want to take advantage of all the core competencies of the cloud.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, Migrate to Google Cloud: Get started, “Replatform: lift and optimize”

notes.front: What is a refactor migration (move and improve)?
notes.back: Modifying workloads to take advantage of cloud capabilities, not just to make them work in the new environment.
notes.explanation: Each workload can be improved for performance, features, cost and user experience.
notes.example: Like a replatform, but the code itself is changed: an app is edited so that it keeps its session data outside the server and can run on several instances.
notes.evidence: In a refactor migration, you modify the workloads to take advantage of cloud capabilities, and not just modify the workloads to make them work in the new environment. You can improve each workload for performance, features, cost, and user experience.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, Migrate to Google Cloud: Get started, “Refactor: move and improve”

notes.front: What is a re-architect migration (continue to modernise)?
notes.back: A migration like a refactor, except that it changes how the workload code functions, not just how it is structured.
notes.explanation: The code changes aim at cloud-optimised properties such as scalability, security and agility.
notes.example: Like a refactor that goes further: a report job that ran once a night is changed to update as each record arrives.
notes.evidence: Re-architect migrations are similar to refactor migrations. However, instead of restructuring how the workload code works, re-architect migrations change how that code functions. Those code changes optimize the workload and take advantage of cloud-optimized properties such as scalability, security, and agility.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, Migrate to Google Cloud: Get started, “Re-architect: continue to modernize”

notes.front: What is a rebuild migration (remove and replace)?
notes.back: Decommissioning an existing app and completely redesigning and rewriting it as a fully cloud-optimised app.
notes.explanation: The guide offers it when the current app is not meeting your goals, for example when it is too costly to migrate in any of the other ways.
notes.example: Like demolishing an old house and building a new one on the plot, instead of renovating.
notes.evidence: In a rebuild migration, you decommission an existing app and completely redesign and rewrite it as a fully cloud-optimized app. If the current app isn't meeting your goals—for example, you don't want to maintain it, it's too costly to migrate using one of the previously mentioned approaches, or it's not supported on Google Cloud—you can do a rebuild migration.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, Migrate to Google Cloud: Get started, “Rebuild: remove and replace”

notes.front: What is a repurchase migration?
notes.back: Moving from a purchased on-premises workload to a cloud-hosted software-as-a-service equivalent.
notes.explanation: The guide’s example is replacing on-premises collaboration software and local storage with Google Workspace.
notes.example: Like cancelling the lease on your own delivery van and paying a courier instead: someone else runs the service.
notes.evidence: A repurchase migration is when you move from a purchased on-premises workload to a cloud-hosted software-as-a-service (SaaS) equivalent. For example, you can move from on-premises collaboration software and local storage to Google Workspace.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, Migrate to Google Cloud: Get started, “Repurchase”

notes.front: What is the Google Cloud Adoption Framework?
notes.back: A map of where your organisation’s technology capabilities are now, and a guide to where you want them to be.
notes.explanation: You use it before migrating to assess your readiness for Google Cloud and which gaps and competencies to work on.
notes.example: Like a fitness assessment before a training plan: it shows your starting level and what to build up.
notes.evidence: The Google Cloud Adoption Framework serves both as a map for determining where your business information technology capabilities are now, and as a guide to where you want to be. You can use this framework to assess your organization's readiness for Google Cloud and what you need to do to fill in the gaps and develop new competencies
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, Migrate to Google Cloud: Get started, “Google Cloud Adoption Framework”

notes.front: What is Migration Center?
notes.back: Google Cloud’s unified platform for the end-to-end journey from on-premises or other cloud environments to Google Cloud.
notes.explanation: It brings cloud spend estimation, asset discovery and tooling for different migration scenarios together.
notes.example: Like a removal firm’s survey visit: it lists what you own and prices the move before anything is packed.
notes.evidence: Google Cloud Migration Center is a unified platform that helps you accelerate your end-to-end cloud journey from your current on-premises or other cloud environments to Google Cloud. With features like cloud spend estimation, asset discovery of your current environment, and a variety of tooling for different migration scenarios
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, Migration Center overview, “Migration Center overview”

notes.front: What does Migrate to Virtual Machines do?
notes.back: It migrates virtual machine instances and their disks from other environments to instances or Persistent Disk volumes on Google Cloud.
notes.explanation: Its sources include on-premises vSphere data centres, other public clouds and Google Cloud VMware Engine.
notes.example: Like a removal van for servers: a server is copied across and started again as a cloud instance.
notes.evidence: Migrate to Virtual Machines lets you migrate virtual machine (VM) instances and disks of VMs from different migration sources such as vSphere on-premises data center, AWS cloud computing services, Azure cloud computing services, and Google Cloud VMware Engine to VM instances or Persistent Disk volumes on Google Cloud.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, Migrate to Virtual Machines documentation, “Migrate to Virtual Machines documentation”

notes.front: What is Database Migration Service (DMS)?
notes.back: Database Migration Service (DMS): a Google Cloud service that migrates databases into Cloud SQL and AlloyDB for PostgreSQL.
notes.explanation: It streamlines networking, manages the initial snapshot and ongoing replication, and reports status throughout the migration.
notes.example: Like a removal firm for one database: a self-managed database on a rented server is copied into a managed service.
notes.evidence: Database Migration Service helps you migrate your data to Google Cloud. The service supports database migrations into Cloud SQL and AlloyDB for PostgreSQL instances. Database Migration Service streamlines networking, manages the initial snapshot and ongoing replication, and provides status updates throughout the migration process.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, Database Migration Service overview, “Database Migration Service overview”

notes.front: What is a conversion workspace in Database Migration Service?
notes.back: The place where DMS converts a source database’s schema and objects into a format the destination database accepts, for heterogeneous migrations.
notes.explanation: The first schema conversion happens automatically as soon as you create the workspace.
notes.example: Like a translator’s first draft that you then edit: table definitions written for one database engine are rewritten for another.
notes.evidence: For heterogeneous migrations, Database Migration Service converts the schema and objects from your source database into a format that is compatible with your destination database. Conversion workspaces offer the following features: Initial schema conversion that happens automatically, once you create your conversion workspace.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, Database Migration Service overview, “Accelerate code and schema conversion with Gemini”

notes.front: Successful migrations change the workload to migrate {{c1::as little as possible}} during the migration operations.
notes.explanation: The guide warns that moving a legacy on-premises workload to a cloud-optimised environment can be challenging and risky.
notes.evidence: Migrating a workload from a legacy on-premises environment or private hosting environment to a cloud-optimized environment, such as a public cloud, can be challenging and risky. Successful migrations change the workload to migrate as little as possible during the migration operations.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, Migrate to Google Cloud: Get started, “Beginning the journey”

notes.front: A rehost migration requires the least amount of time because {{c1::the amount of refactoring is kept to a minimum}}.
notes.explanation: Less refactoring means less work before the workload can run in the target environment.
notes.evidence: This migration is the type that requires the least amount of time because the amount of refactoring is kept to a minimum.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, Migrate to Google Cloud: Get started, “Rehost: lift and shift”

notes.front: When must you use a rehost migration, whatever you would prefer?
notes.back: When you can neither refactor the workload nor decommission it.
notes.explanation: Technical issues can force it: for example, the workload’s source code may be difficult or impossible to modify.
notes.evidence: If you cannot refactor a workload to migrate and cannot decommission the workload, you must use a rehost migration. For example, it can be difficult or impossible to modify the source code of the workload
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, Migrate to Google Cloud: Get started, “Rehost: lift and shift”

notes.front: What is the drawback of a rehost migration once the workload runs in the target environment?
notes.back: It isn’t optimised for the cloud, so it doesn’t take full advantage of features such as horizontal scalability and highly managed services.
notes.explanation: Fine-grained pricing is a third cloud platform feature that such workloads don’t fully use.
notes.evidence: However, after a rehost migration, the workloads that are running in the target environment aren't optimized for the cloud. These workloads don't take full advantage of cloud platform features, such as horizontal scalability, fine-grained pricing, and highly managed services.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, Migrate to Google Cloud: Get started, “Rehost: lift and shift”

notes.front: Why does a replatform migration need several rounds of testing?
notes.back: The new cloud platform has a different underlying codebase, and testing makes sure everything runs at its optimal level.
notes.explanation: This is part of why the guide says replatforming takes more work than rehosting.
notes.evidence: However, replatform migrations take more work to accomplish than rehost migrations. The new cloud platform will have a different underlying codebase, which requires several rounds of testing to make sure that everything is running at its optimal level.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, Migrate to Google Cloud: Get started, “Replatform: lift and optimize”

notes.front: What are two reasons the guide gives for choosing a refactor migration?
notes.back: The app’s architecture or infrastructure isn’t supported in the target as it is; or a major update is needed besides the migration changes.
notes.explanation: In the first case, some refactoring is needed simply to overcome the limits of the target environment.
notes.evidence: If the current architecture or infrastructure of an app isn't supported in the target environment as it is, a certain amount of refactoring is necessary to overcome these limits. Another reason to choose the refactor approach is when a major update to the workload is necessary in addition to the updates you need to make to migrate.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, Migrate to Google Cloud: Get started, “Refactor: move and improve”

notes.front: What example does the guide give of a re-architect migration?
notes.back: Turning one large, monolithic workload into several independent microservices deployed on Google Cloud.
notes.explanation: Changes like this aim at cloud-optimised properties such as scalability, security and agility.
notes.evidence: Those code changes optimize the workload and take advantage of cloud-optimized properties such as scalability, security, and agility. For example, a re-architect migration can take one large, monolithic workload and turn it into several independent microservices that you deploy on Google Cloud.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, Migrate to Google Cloud: Get started, “Re-architect: continue to modernize”

notes.front: Why does a re-architect migration need several rounds of testing?
notes.back: It can potentially introduce bugs or security issues into the new workloads.
notes.explanation: It is also more complex than a refactor migration, so it takes more time and effort.
notes.evidence: A re-architect migration is more complex than a refactor migration, so it takes more time and effort. A re-architect migration can also potentially introduce bugs or security issues into the new workloads. Thus, a re-architect migration requires several rounds of testing
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, Migrate to Google Cloud: Get started, “Re-architect: continue to modernize”

notes.front: What does a rebuild migration remove, according to the guide, because the app is rewritten from scratch?
notes.back: The technical debt of the existing, legacy version of the app.
notes.explanation: The rewritten app can also take full advantage of features such as horizontal scalability, highly managed services and high availability.
notes.evidence: Rebuild migrations let your app take full advantage of Google Cloud features, such as horizontal scalability, highly managed services, and high availability. Because you're rewriting the app from scratch, you also remove the technical debt of the existing, legacy version.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, Migrate to Google Cloud: Get started, “Rebuild: remove and replace”

notes.front: For which kind of app is a rebuild migration not suitable?
notes.back: Ready-made apps, because a rebuild requires rewriting the app.
notes.explanation: For any app you rebuild, you also need to weigh the extra time and effort of redesigning and rewriting it.
notes.evidence: Moreover, this type of migration isn't suitable for ready-made apps because it requires rewriting the app. You need to evaluate the extra time and effort to redesign and rewrite the app as part of its lifecycle.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, Migrate to Google Cloud: Get started, “Rebuild: remove and replace”

notes.front: What trade-off does the guide describe for a repurchase migration?
notes.back: It might be much easier on resources than refactoring, rebuilding or re-architecting, but it might cost a lot more and give less granular control.
notes.explanation: Both sides carry the guide’s “might”: neither the saving in effort nor the extra cost is certain.
notes.evidence: From a resources perspective, a repurchase migration might be a lot easier than refactoring, rebuilding, or re-architecting. However, a repurchase migration might be a lot more expensive and you might not get the granular features of controlling your own cloud environments.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, Migrate to Google Cloud: Get started, “Repurchase”

notes.front: In which phase of the migration path do you perform total cost of ownership calculations and establish app performance benchmarks?
notes.back: Assess.
notes.explanation: It is the first of the four phases, and it also identifies app dependencies and requirements.
notes.evidence: There are four phases of your migration: Assess. In this phase, you perform a thorough assessment and discovery of your existing environment in order to understand your app and environment inventory, identify app dependencies and requirements, perform total cost of ownership calculations, and establish app performance benchmarks.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, Migrate to Google Cloud: Get started, “The migration path”

notes.front: In which migration phase do you design, implement and execute the process that moves workloads to Google Cloud?
notes.back: Deploy.
notes.explanation: During this phase you might also have to refine your cloud infrastructure to deal with new needs.
notes.evidence: Deploy. In this phase, you design, implement and execute a deployment process to move workloads to Google Cloud. You might also have to refine your cloud infrastructure to deal with new needs.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, Migrate to Google Cloud: Get started, “The migration path”

notes.front: In which migration phase do you begin to take full advantage of cloud-optimised technologies and capabilities?
notes.back: Optimise.
notes.explanation: The guide links this phase to gains in performance, scalability, disaster recovery and costs, among others.
notes.evidence: Optimize. In this phase, you begin to take full advantage of cloud-optimized technologies and capabilities to expand your business's potential to things such as performance, scalability, disaster recovery, costs, training
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, Migrate to Google Cloud: Get started, “The migration path”

notes.front: Which Google Cloud Adoption Framework theme measures how far your technology departments have a mandate from leadership to migrate?
notes.back: Lead.
notes.explanation: It is one of the framework’s four themes, with Learn, Scale and Secure.
notes.evidence: The framework assesses four themes: Learn. The quality and scale of your learning programs. Lead. The extent to which your IT departments are supported by a mandate from leadership to migrate to Google Cloud.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, Migrate to Google Cloud: Get started, “Google Cloud Adoption Framework”

notes.front: In the Google Cloud Adoption Framework, which phase fits an organisation with no coherent plan across its workloads that mostly wants a quick return on investment?
notes.back: Tactical.
notes.explanation: It is the first of three phases a theme can be in, before Strategic and Transformational.
notes.evidence: For each theme, you should be in one of the following three phases, according to the framework: Tactical. There are no coherent plans covering all the individual workloads you have in place. You're mostly interested in a quick return on investments and little disruption to your IT organization.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, Migrate to Google Cloud: Get started, “Google Cloud Adoption Framework”

notes.front: What does Migration Center base its rapid estimate of future Google Cloud costs on?
notes.back: The size and configuration of your current on-premises or other cloud resources.
notes.explanation: Because it starts from resources you already run, it gives a quick first price for the move; the documentation marks the feature Preview, so it may change.
notes.evidence: Migration Center lets you generate a rapid cost estimate of future Google Cloud costs based on the size and configuration of your current on-premises or other cloud environment resources (Preview).
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, Migration Center overview, “Estimate your cloud costs”

notes.front: How does Migration Center build an inventory of on-premises assets such as servers and databases?
notes.back: By automatically scanning your on-premises environment.
notes.explanation: Automating the inventory saves the time and energy that collecting the data by hand would take.
notes.evidence: Migration Center helps you create an inventory of your assets, including servers, Microsoft SQL Server, MySQL, and PostgreSQL databases, by automatically scanning your on-premises environment. By automating as much of this as possible with Migration Center, it saves your organization time and energy that would otherwise be spent collecting this data manually.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, Migration Center overview, “Discover your assets”

notes.front: In Migration Center, what are total cost of ownership reports based on?
notes.back: The migration preferences you specify, according to your business objectives and constraints.
notes.explanation: The reports are part of the assessment, which gives a holistic view of your environment.
notes.evidence: With Migration Center, you can dive deep in the analysis and get a holistic view into your environment. Generate total cost of ownership reports based on the migration preferences that you specify according to your business objectives and constraints.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, Migration Center overview, “Assess your infrastructure”

notes.front: Which migration strategies do Migration Center’s migration tools support, as the overview names them?
notes.back: Rehost, replatform and refactor, among a variety of others.
notes.explanation: Migration Center does not stop at assessment: it also offers tools for moving the infrastructure itself.
notes.evidence: When you need to migrate your infrastructure to Google Cloud, Migration Center can help you with many different tools that support a variety of migration strategies like rehost, replatform, and refactor.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, Migration Center overview, “Migrate”

notes.front: In a continuous DMS migration, switching over when source and destination are {{c1::in sync}} gives minimal downtime.
notes.explanation: Once replication is finalised, the destination is ready to be used as a standalone primary instance.
notes.evidence: When the destination is ready for reads and writes, you finalize replication between the source and the destination. The destination Cloud SQL instance or AlloyDB for PostgreSQL cluster is then ready to be used as a standalone primary instance. Doing the switch when the source and destination are in sync gives you minimal downtime.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, Database Migration Service overview, “Continuous migration”

notes.front: Why can applications see downtime during a one-time Database Migration Service migration?
notes.back: There can be no new writes to the source database while the migration is in progress.
notes.explanation: A one-time migration is a dump and load: the destination is ready to use only when the load completes.
notes.evidence: This process is a dump and load, where the destination is ready to be used when the load completes. Any applications that depend on the source database can experience downtime during the migration process because there can be no new writes to this database while the migration is in progress.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, Database Migration Service overview, “One-time migration”

notes.front: What process does Database Migration Service’s continuous replication rely on after the initial snapshot?
notes.back: Change data capture: it identifies and captures only the changes, such as inserts, updates and deletes, made after the snapshot.
notes.explanation: Replicating only modifications is more efficient than replicating the entire database frequently, which helps minimise downtime.
notes.evidence: It's based on Change Data Capture (CDC), a process that identifies and captures only the changes, such as inserts, updates, deletes that you made to the database after the initial snapshot is taken. Such an approach minimises downtime for the following reasons: Continuous replication is more efficient than replicating the entire database frequently, as it only focuses on modifications.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, Database Migration Service overview, “Minimal downtime”

notes.front: Does Database Migration Service support writing to and reading from both the source and the destination during a migration?
notes.back: No. It doesn’t support such a dual-write scenario.
notes.explanation: Its multi-cloud use case is different: it replicates continuously into Google Cloud for read availability.
notes.evidence: Much like the read replicas across regions, if data exists in another cloud provider, a migration job can continuously replicate the database into Google Cloud for multi-cloud read-availability. Database Migration Service doesn't support a dual-write scenario, that is writing to and reading from both the source and destination.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, Database Migration Service overview, “Use cases”

notes.front: In a conversion workspace, {{c1::customisation directives}} let you override the rules of automated schema conversion.
notes.explanation: The workspace also offers an interactive editor for fixing conversion issues, and assistance from Gemini conversion features.
notes.evidence: The interactive SQL editor that helps you fix conversion issues or adjust the schema to better fit your needs. Assistance of Gemini conversion features. Customization directives that you can use to override the rules of automated schema conversion.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, Database Migration Service overview, “Accelerate code and schema conversion with Gemini”

notes.front: Before moving migration data over the public internet, whom should you check with, and about what?
notes.back: Your security administrator, about whether company policy forbids such transfers.
notes.explanation: Check too whether that connection carries production traffic: large-scale transfers might hurt the production network’s performance.
notes.evidence: If you opt for an approach that involves transferring data over the public internet, we recommend that you check with your security administrator on whether your company policy forbids such transfers. Also, check whether the public internet connection is used for your production traffic. Finally, consider that large-scale data transfers might negatively impact the performance of your production network.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, Migrate to Google Cloud: Transfer your large datasets, “Increasing network bandwidth”

notes.front: When collecting requirements for a data transfer, what might stop a dataset from being moved at all?
notes.back: Regulatory, security or other factors that prohibit transferring it.
notes.explanation: Other data may need transforming first, for example to remove sensitive data, with a product such as Dataflow or Cloud Data Fusion.
notes.evidence: Identify what datasets you can move. Consider whether regulatory, security, or other factors prohibit some datasets from being transferred. If you need to transform some of your data before you move it (for example, to remove sensitive data or reorganize your data), consider using a data integration product like Dataflow or Cloud Data Fusion
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, Migrate to Google Cloud: Transfer your large datasets, “Step 2: Collecting requirements and available resources”

notes.front: Why is the data-access microservice approach lighter than the Y (writing and reading) approach?
notes.back: Its refactoring effort is focused on the data-access microservice alone.
notes.explanation: Like the Y approach, though, it still places most of the burden on the development side.
notes.evidence: Like the Y (writing and reading) approach, the data-access microservice approach places most of the burden on the development side. However, it's significantly lighter compared to the Y (writing and reading) approach, because the refactoring efforts are focused on the data-access microservice.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, Migrate to Google Cloud: Transfer your large datasets, “Data-access microservice”

notes.front: How do sole-tenant nodes help with bring-your-own-licence software licensed per core or per processor?
notes.back: They give some visibility into the underlying hardware, so you can track core and processor usage.
notes.explanation: They can also meet the dedicated hardware requirements that such licences carry.
notes.evidence: Sole-tenant nodes can help you meet dedicated hardware requirements for bring your own license (BYOL) scenarios that require per-core or per-processor licenses. When you use sole-tenant nodes, you have some visibility into the underlying hardware, which lets you track core and processor usage.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, Sole-tenancy overview (Compute Engine), “Sole-tenancy overview”

notes.front: Which sole-tenant host maintenance policy suits a fault-tolerant workload, licensed by physical cores, that can take about an hour of downtime during host events?
notes.back: The Restart in place policy.
notes.explanation: It also suits workloads that must stay on the same physical server or that don’t require live migration.
notes.evidence: This policy is most suitable for workloads that are fault-tolerant and can experience approximately one hour of downtime during host events, workloads that must remain on the same physical server, workloads that don't require live migration, or if you have licenses that are based on the number of physical cores or processors.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, Sole-tenancy overview (Compute Engine), “Restart in place host maintenance policy”

notes.front: A company’s in-house expense app is not supported on Google Cloud, and nobody wants to keep maintaining its code. The company wants a new, fully cloud-optimised app of its own. Which migration type fits?
notes.back: B: rebuild.
notes.choices:
A) Rehost
B) Rebuild
C) Replatform
D) Repurchase
notes.choicesExplained: A) Rehost moves the app with minimal change, keeping the code no one wants to maintain. C) Replatform lifts the existing app and then optimises it, so the old app survives. D) Repurchase buys a hosted equivalent instead of producing the company’s own new app.
notes.explanation: The guide offers a rebuild when the current app isn’t meeting your goals, for example when you don’t want to maintain it or it isn’t supported on Google Cloud.
notes.evidence: In a rebuild migration, you decommission an existing app and completely redesign and rewrite it as a fully cloud-optimized app. If the current app isn't meeting your goals—for example, you don't want to maintain it, it's too costly to migrate using one of the previously mentioned approaches, or it's not supported on Google Cloud—you can do a rebuild migration.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, Migrate to Google Cloud: Get started, “Rebuild: remove and replace”

notes.front: A firm runs a customer-relationship package it bought from a vendor on its own servers. It wants to switch to the vendor’s hosted software-as-a-service version and accepts less control. Which migration type is this?
notes.back: B: repurchase.
notes.choices:
A) Rehost
B) Repurchase
C) Refactor
D) Re-architect
notes.choicesExplained: A) Rehost moves the firm’s own installation to the cloud; the firm would still run it. C) Refactor modifies workloads the firm keeps running. D) Re-architect changes how the firm’s own code functions.
notes.explanation: Moving from a purchased on-premises workload to a hosted equivalent is the guide’s definition of a repurchase.
notes.evidence: A repurchase migration is when you move from a purchased on-premises workload to a cloud-hosted software-as-a-service (SaaS) equivalent.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, Migrate to Google Cloud: Get started, “Repurchase”

notes.front: The source code of a vendor-built stock-control tool was lost years ago, yet the business cannot retire the tool. It must move to Google Cloud. Which migration type must be used?
notes.back: D: rehost.
notes.choices:
A) Refactor
B) Re-architect
C) Rebuild
D) Rehost
notes.choicesExplained: A) Refactor and B) re-architect both require modifying the code, which no one can do. C) Rebuild decommissions the tool and rewrites it, but the business wants this tool kept.
notes.explanation: The guide says that if you cannot refactor a workload and cannot decommission it, you must rehost it.
notes.evidence: If you cannot refactor a workload to migrate and cannot decommission the workload, you must use a rehost migration. For example, it can be difficult or impossible to modify the source code of the workload
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, Migrate to Google Cloud: Get started, “Rehost: lift and shift”

notes.front: During its move, a reservation system’s code will be changed in how it functions, not merely restructured, to gain agility and security. The team plans several rounds of testing. Which migration type is it?
notes.back: D: re-architect.
notes.choices:
A) Refactor
B) Repurchase
C) Rehost
D) Re-architect
notes.choicesExplained: A) Refactor restructures how the code works; changing how it functions goes further. C) Rehost makes only the minimum changes needed to run. B) Repurchase replaces the system with a hosted product instead of changing its code.
notes.explanation: Changing how the code functions, to gain cloud-optimised properties such as security and agility, is what defines a re-architect migration.
notes.evidence: Re-architect migrations are similar to refactor migrations. However, instead of restructuring how the workload code works, re-architect migrations change how that code functions. Those code changes optimize the workload and take advantage of cloud-optimized properties such as scalability, security, and agility.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, Migrate to Google Cloud: Get started, “Re-architect: continue to modernize”

notes.front: A team lifts an existing web app into Google Cloud and then optimises it for elastic computing and redundancy, without rewriting it from scratch. Which migration type is this?
notes.back: B: replatform.
notes.choices:
A) Rehost
B) Replatform
C) Rebuild
D) Repurchase
notes.choicesExplained: A) Rehost stops after the move, with only the minimum changes. C) Rebuild rewrites the app from scratch, which the team isn’t doing. D) Repurchase swaps the app for a hosted product.
notes.explanation: Lifting and then optimising, to use cloud competencies such as elastic computing and redundancy, is what the guide calls replatforming.
notes.evidence: In a replatform migration, you lift the existing workloads and then optimize them for the new cloud environment. A replatform migration is best for organizations that want to take advantage of all the core competencies of the cloud. These competencies include elastic computing, redundancy, improved performance, and security.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, Migrate to Google Cloud: Get started, “Replatform: lift and optimize”

notes.front: An app’s current architecture isn’t supported by the target environment as it is. The team will modify it to overcome that and improve its performance and cost, without rewriting it from scratch. Which migration type is this?
notes.back: B: refactor.
notes.choices:
A) Rehost
B) Refactor
C) Rebuild
D) Repurchase
notes.choicesExplained: A) Rehost cannot work, because the architecture isn’t supported as it is. C) Rebuild rewrites the app completely. D) Repurchase replaces it with a hosted product instead of modifying it.
notes.explanation: An unsupported architecture needs some refactoring to overcome the target’s limits, and refactoring can also improve performance and cost.
notes.evidence: If the current architecture or infrastructure of an app isn't supported in the target environment as it is, a certain amount of refactoring is necessary to overcome these limits.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, Migrate to Google Cloud: Get started, “Refactor: move and improve”

notes.front: A migration team has finished its inventory and is now deciding identity management, the organisation and project structure, networking and the order in which apps will move. Which phase is it in?
notes.back: A: plan.
notes.choices:
A) Plan
B) Assess
C) Deploy
D) Optimise
notes.choicesExplained: B) Assess is the inventory and discovery work the team has finished. C) Deploy executes the moves once the plan exists. D) Optimise comes after workloads are in Google Cloud.
notes.explanation: The guide puts identity management, organisation and project structure, networking and a prioritised strategy in the Plan phase.
notes.evidence: Plan. In this phase, you create the basic cloud infrastructure for your workloads to live in and plan how you will move apps. This planning includes identity management, organization and project structure, networking, sorting your apps, and developing a prioritized migration strategy.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, Migrate to Google Cloud: Get started, “The migration path”

notes.front: Before moving a group of on-premises servers, an architect needs to know which components must be migrated together. Which Migration Center feature set helps?
notes.back: B: assess your infrastructure.
notes.choices:
A) Estimate your cloud costs
B) Assess your infrastructure
C) Migrate
D) Discover your assets
notes.choicesExplained: A) The cost estimate prices future Google Cloud use; it doesn’t map dependencies. D) Discovery builds the inventory of assets, not the links between them. C) The migrate tools carry out the move after the planning.
notes.explanation: The assessment identifies application and network dependencies so that you know which components to move together.
notes.evidence: Identify application and network dependencies to know which components you must migrate together.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, Migration Center overview, “Assess your infrastructure”

notes.front: A company wants to move the virtual machines of its on-premises vSphere estate, with their disks, onto instances on Google Cloud. Which service fits?
notes.back: A: Migrate to Virtual Machines.
notes.choices:
A) Migrate to Virtual Machines
B) Database Migration Service
C) Storage Transfer Service
D) Migration Center’s cost estimate
notes.choicesExplained: B) DMS moves databases into Cloud SQL and AlloyDB for PostgreSQL, not whole machines. C) Storage Transfer Service moves data, not running machines. D) The cost estimate prices the move but moves nothing.
notes.explanation: An on-premises vSphere data centre is one of the sources that Migrate to Virtual Machines supports.
notes.evidence: Migrate to Virtual Machines lets you migrate virtual machine (VM) instances and disks of VMs from different migration sources such as vSphere on-premises data center
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, Migrate to Virtual Machines documentation, “Migrate to Virtual Machines documentation”

notes.front: An online booking database must stay writable while it moves to Cloud SQL, with only a brief switch-over at the end. Which approach in Database Migration Service fits?
notes.back: A: a continuous migration.
notes.choices:
A) A continuous migration
B) Writing to and reading from both databases during the move
C) A one-time migration
D) Any heterogeneous migration
notes.choicesExplained: C) A one-time migration blocks new writes to the source while it runs. B) DMS doesn’t support a dual-write scenario. D) Heterogeneous describes different database engines, not how downtime is kept low.
notes.explanation: Changes keep flowing after the initial dump and load, and switching once the two are in sync gives minimal downtime.
notes.evidence: Continuous (sometimes referred to as ongoing or online) migration is a continuous flow of changes from your source to your destination that follows an initial full dump and load.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, Database Migration Service overview, “Continuous migration”

notes.front: An Oracle database will move to AlloyDB for PostgreSQL with Database Migration Service. What kind of migration is it, and what converts its schema?
notes.back: C: heterogeneous; a conversion workspace.
notes.choices:
A) Homogeneous; no conversion is needed
B) Homogeneous; a conversion workspace
C) Heterogeneous; a conversion workspace
D) Heterogeneous; Migrate to Virtual Machines
notes.choicesExplained: B) and A) Homogeneous means the same database technology at both ends, and Oracle and PostgreSQL differ. D) Migrate to Virtual Machines moves machines and disks; it converts no schema.
notes.explanation: Source and destination technologies differ, and in heterogeneous migrations DMS converts the schema and objects in a conversion workspace.
notes.evidence: Unlike homogeneous migrations, in heterogeneous migrations, such as Oracle to Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL, the database technology of the source and destination are different.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, Database Migration Service overview, “Heterogeneous migrations”

notes.front: A highly available workload on sole-tenant nodes runs software whose licences are based on the number of physical cores. Which host maintenance policy fits?
notes.back: C: migrate within node group.
notes.choices:
A) Default
B) Restart in place
C) Migrate within node group
D) No policy: move the workload to Spot VMs
notes.choicesExplained: A) Default lets instances live migrate to any server, so it can’t keep physical core use down. B) Restart in place means about an hour of downtime, which a highly available workload can’t take. D) Spot VMs are not dedicated hardware.
notes.explanation: Each node in the group is pinned to a fixed set of physical servers, while live migration keeps the workload running.
notes.evidence: This policy is most suitable for high-availability workloads with licenses that are based on the number of physical cores or processors, because with this host maintenance policy, each sole-tenant node in the group is pinned to a fixed set of physical servers
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, Sole-tenancy overview (Compute Engine), “Migrate within node group host maintenance policy”

notes.front: A workload has hard high-availability requirements and cannot afford any cut-over window while its data migrates. Which data migration approach does the guide point to?
notes.back: C: Y (writing and reading).
notes.choices:
A) Scheduled maintenance
B) Continuous replication
C) Y (writing and reading)
D) A single dump and load
notes.choicesExplained: A) Scheduled maintenance needs a planned cut-over window. B) Continuous replication shortens the window but still needs one. D) A dump and load blocks writes while it runs.
notes.explanation: In the Y approach the workload writes and reads data in both the legacy site and the new site during the migration.
notes.evidence: If your workloads have hard high-availability requirements and you cannot afford the downtime represented by a cut-over window, you need to take a different approach. For this scenario, you can use an approach that in this document is referred to as Y (writing and reading), which is a form of parallel migration.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, Migrate to Google Cloud: Transfer your large datasets, “Y (writing and reading)”

notes.front: How do legacy workloads differ from cloud-optimised ones, in the migration guide’s terms?
notes.back: Legacy workloads usually don’t support any scalability. Cloud-optimised ones are natively scalable, portable, available and secure.
notes.explanation: The missing scalability is why legacy workloads can be difficult to modify and expensive to run and maintain.
notes.evidence: These workloads and operations can be difficult to modify and expensive to run and maintain because they usually don't support any type of scalability. Cloud-optimized workloads and operations are natively scalable, portable, available, and secure.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, Migrate to Google Cloud: Get started, “Beginning the journey”

notes.front: What separates a homogeneous from a heterogeneous database migration?
notes.back: Homogeneous: the same database technology at source and destination. Heterogeneous: different technologies.
notes.explanation: The documentation’s homogeneous example is MySQL to Cloud SQL for MySQL.
notes.evidence: Homogeneous migrations take place when you migrate data between the same database technology. For example, from MySQL to Cloud SQL for MySQL.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, Database Migration Service overview, “Homogeneous migrations”

notes.front: How does the continuous replication approach to data migration compare with scheduled maintenance?
notes.back: It is more complex, but it minimises the cut-over window.
notes.explanation: It leaves less data to synchronise at the end, which is what shortens the cut-over window.
notes.evidence: The continuous replication approach (also called online migration or trickle migration) is more complex than the scheduled maintenance approach. However, the continuous replication approach minimizes the time for the required cut-over window, because it minimizes the amount of data that you need to synchronize.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, Migrate to Google Cloud: Transfer your large datasets, “Continuous replication”
